\title{Medora: a consent-gated assistive-AI layer over an open Bangladesh medicine
reference for bilingual health-record software}

\author{Sarwad Hasan Siddiqui}
\author{Adiba Tahsin}
\author{Kazi Saeed Alam\corref{cor1}}
\ead{saeed.alam@cse.kuet.ac.bd}
\cortext[cor1]{Corresponding author.}
\address{Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Khulna University of Engineering \& Technology, Khulna 9203, Bangladesh}

\begin{abstract}
Assistive language models are reaching health software faster than the structures meant to
contain them. Medora is open-source research software that makes those structures explicit,
joining bilingual English/Bengali patient-held records and appointment coordination to an
assistive-AI layer of twenty-one endpoints. Its safety properties are structural, not
prompt-dependent. External calls need a purpose-specific revocable grant and pass bilingual
redaction and pseudonymisation, assistant navigation resolves through an immutable
role-scoped registry holding no administrative routes, and summary items can cite only
records the backend supplied. Routing, consent, and red-flag detection involve no model.
Under all of it sits an open Bangladesh medicine reference of
7{,}389 drugs and 67{,}001 brands, built from five published datasets by one script. We
report what was measured and name what was not. Medora is not clinically validated and is
not a medical device.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
digital health \sep assistive AI \sep consent-gated processing \sep
medicine reference data \sep deterministic intent routing \sep bilingual software
\end{keyword}
\end{frontmatter}

\section{Motivation and significance}

Medora addresses a practical research problem. How can a bilingual web platform put
language-model assistance in front of patients and clinicians without letting it become
unreviewed clinical authority? Such features are cheap to add and hard to bound, and the
bounding is the engineering problem. The intended users are
health-informatics researchers, software-engineering educators, and teams studying consent,
assistive-AI containment, or concurrency.

Bangladesh has a long-running national digital-health program, but studies describe uneven
eHealth implementation and clinician concerns about electronic-record
adoption~\cite{ahmed2014,khan2012}. That motivates an inspectable artifact for bilingual,
patient-held workflows. It does not make Medora representative of Bangladesh or fit for
deployment.

Two contributions carry most of the reuse value. The first is an open medicine reference
for a market with none. Drug terminology services such as RxNorm underpin much clinical
software, but their coverage is national and Bangladesh is not among the markets
served~\cite{rxnorm}. Medora consolidates five published datasets into a normalized
three-table reference and ships the script that builds it.

The second is a containment pattern for assistive AI. Consent is checked before a call
leaves the deployment. Assistant navigation resolves against a fixed registry, so the set
of destinations a model can reach is readable from one file and cannot grow at inference
time. The backend attaches summary source references after schema validation, which makes
a fabricated citation structurally impossible rather than unlikely. Most safety-critical
logic is deterministic (Table~\ref{tab:components}).

Established open-source systems cover a wider institutional scope. OpenMRS, Bahmni, and GNU
Health provide modular medical-record, hospital, laboratory, and Fast Healthcare
Interoperability Resources (FHIR) capabilities~\cite{openmrs,bahmni,gnuhealth}. Medora is a
smaller mobile-oriented implementation linking patient-held records and booking to an
inspectable assistive-AI layer (Table~\ref{tab:related-work}). They are complements, not
performance baselines.

Clinical summarization work shows that fluency is not enough, and that faithfulness and
traceability need separate evaluation~\cite{shing2021,tracsum}. Symptom-checker studies
report wide variation in diagnostic and urgency recommendations~\cite{wallace2022}. Medora
therefore avoids diagnosis and triage. It offers specialty candidates for navigation, keeps
manual browsing, and runs deterministic emergency rules before any model call.

\section{Software description}

\subsection{Software architecture}

Medora is a Next.js web client, a FastAPI core API, a separate FastAPI OCR service, and
PostgreSQL (Fig.~\ref{fig:trust}). Authentication identifies the actor. Backend role,
ownership, care-relationship, appointment-state, and consent checks authorize each
operation, and frontend visibility is only a usability aid.

Those predicates live in the API, so they hold only while the API is the sole path to the
data. A release audit found it was not. The managed database also exposed a direct data API
where every table granted the anonymous role full read and write access with row-level
security off, so the browser-published anonymous key reached patient rows without passing
any check above. The permission matrix and its negative tests missed it because they
exercised the API alone. The release revokes those grants, turns on row-level security
everywhere, and narrows the client's only direct subscription to a trigger-maintained change
feed. An authorization model written entirely in application code depends on the database
having no second door, and that assumption deserves its own test.

\begin{figure}[!h]
\centering\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{figures-src/trust_boundary.tex}}
\caption{Deployment and trust boundaries. Local speech recognition and OCR cross no
external boundary. Hosted text models, Vapi live audio, and Azure OCR are separate
recipients with separate grants.}
\label{fig:trust}
\end{figure}

Processing is deny-by-default (Fig.~\ref{fig:consent}). A grant records subject, recipient,
purpose, scopes, policy version, validity, grant and revocation times, and audit metadata.
Missing, expired, revoked, or wrong-scope grants produce a typed denial and offer a local
path where one exists. Revocation blocks later processing but cannot retract what was
already disclosed, and local mode never falls back to a cloud service.

\begin{figure}[!h]
\centering\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{figures-src/consent_flow.tex}}
\caption{Consent-aware processing. Purpose and provider are checked before any external
call; outputs stay non-authoritative drafts.}
\label{fig:consent}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Software functionalities}

\textbf{Medicine reference.} Search, medication linking, prescription composition, and
matching of recognised prescription text all resolve through one medicine identity. A
published script normalizes five datasets into three tables (Table~\ref{tab:corpus}).
\texttt{drugs} holds canonical identity, keyed on generic name, strength, and dosage form,
immutable after creation. \texttt{brands} maps the commercial names a prescriber writes
many-to-one onto those identities. \texttt{medicine\_search\_index} flattens both into one
trigram-indexed term space for typo-tolerant lookup. Dosage logic, interaction checking,
and effectiveness ranking are explicit non-goals.

\begin{table}[!h]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
Artifact & Count \\
\midrule
Consolidated source rows & 71{,}795 \\
Canonical drugs (generic $\times$ strength $\times$ form) & 7{,}389 \\
Brand entries & 67{,}001 \\
Search-index terms & 74{,}390 \\
Distinct generic names & 5{,}242 \\
Distinct brand names & 52{,}117 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Medicine reference as loaded. Counts differ from the consolidated CSV because the
canonical key collapses brand duplicates.}
\label{tab:corpus}
\end{table}

\textbf{Assistive-AI layer.} Twenty-one endpoints expose assistive features
(Table~\ref{tab:ai-surface}), all sharing one pipeline built from the components in
Table~\ref{tab:components}. One orchestrator is the only component that knows which
provider is configured: Groq, Gemini, Cerebras, or a deterministic mock. It recursively
sanitizes input, issues the call under a random correlation identifier rather than a stable
subject token, validates the response against a Pydantic model, and records latency and
provider metadata. Raw prompts, transcripts, and findings are not logged by default, and
validation failure raises instead of degrading to unvalidated prose.

Three guards run before the orchestrator. A consent guard returns the permitted categories,
filters the payload, and prepends a restriction notice when anything was removed, so the
model knows it is reasoning over a partial record. A redaction stage removes emails,
telephone numbers, addresses, national and passport identifiers, account numbers, and dates
in both scripts. A pseudonymiser substitutes a stable opaque patient reference, so raw
identifiers reach neither the provider nor the audit log. Doctor reads of a patient record
also require a care relationship and go to a patient-visible audit.

Chorui, the in-app assistant, is the clearest case of the pattern
(Fig.~\ref{fig:chorui}). An utterance is normalized to a canonical intent, then resolved
against an immutable tuple of typed registry entries binding intent and role scope to a
route, its required parameters, and a fallback. The registry holds 24 entries over 23
canonical intents, 11 patient-scoped and 11 doctor-scoped with 2 shared. Administrative
routes are never registered, and missing parameters produce a clarification, not a guess.
Destinations are fixed at build time and auditable from one file, unlike free-form tool
selection where the prompt is the only control.

\begin{figure}[!h]
\centering\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures-src/chorui_architecture.pdf}
\caption{Chorui request path. Intent normalization and registry resolution are
deterministic. The model contributes phrasing, not the set of reachable destinations.}
\label{fig:chorui}
\end{figure}

Summaries for patients, prescribers, and prescription histories are read-only. The backend
attaches source references after schema validation, so an item can cite only a record the
request supplied, and a request carrying no source record returns a not-found item instead
of model prose. Record timestamps are stripped before the prompt leaves the deployment, so
the model cannot reason about temporal order. A clinician-verification warning stays visible
and nothing writes back automatically.

Local faster-whisper transcription is preloaded at startup and crosses no external
boundary~\cite{whisper}; only the structuring step uses a hosted model. Vapi live audio is a
separate external recipient needing its own grant at capture and again when callbacks are
processed, and local mode never escalates to it.

That last column is this release's main limitation. Structural controls apply uniformly
across all twenty-one endpoints; empirical evidence does not. The six groups without
fixtures are exercised only by contract and authorization tests, and no accuracy should be
inferred for them.

\textbf{Reviewable clinical semantics.} Nothing the layer produces is authoritative.
Summaries are drafts, prescription suggestions pre-fill fields a prescriber edits and signs,
and specialty search returns candidates with manual browse controls. Recognised prescription
images return a draft flagged \texttt{authoritative\_writeback=false} that a person verifies
row by row. A patient's later action is
\texttt{receipt\_acknowledged} or \texttt{discrepancy\_reported}, and neither says a
medicine is appropriate. The service worker caches only versioned static and public
resources, health-data writes are never background-synchronized, and logout clears caches,
IndexedDB, session and sensitive local storage.

\textbf{Appointment transaction and delivery.} Creating an appointment requires an
\texttt{Idempotency-Key}. The backend locks the key and slot, validates availability, and
writes the appointment, idempotency result, audit record, and outbox event in one
transaction, with a uniqueness constraint as the last defense against duplicate active
slots. Only committed outbox events are published, so consistency ends at commit and
propagation is a later event measured separately. After a reconnect, clients re-query
PostgreSQL, which stays authoritative. A background dispatcher turns medication and
appointment reminders into in-app notifications and email; web push is optional and stays
off unless VAPID keys are configured.

\subsection{Evaluation and reproducibility}

Evaluation covers the privacy stack, two AI behaviours with defined correctness criteria,
and booking concurrency. Mock and live results are never pooled.

The privacy suite is a hand-authored synthetic bilingual corpus covering the identifier
groups in Table~\ref{tab:privacy-span-results} together with spacing and misspelling
variants, obfuscated formats, over-redaction controls, consent state, and prompt injection.
The cases were written without reference to the redaction patterns they test, so precision
and recall fall below 100\%. Unlabelled personal names, clinician names in prose,
month-name dates, and obfuscated contact formats go undetected. Each such case carries a
written limitation in the archived results, and the release gate fails on any undisclosed
failure. Reporting 75.5\% instead of tuning the corpus upward is deliberate: it is what
transfers to a deployment.

Navigation fixtures are scored on two paths, a recorded provider intent and the
deterministic mock, against the classifier the request path itself uses. Uncertainty is a
flag next to the candidates, not a fourth exclusive class, and every path asserts that
manual browsing stays available. The red-flag rules are keyword based and also match
negated, third-person, and historical mentions, so they over-trigger toward emergency
guidance; those cases are enumerated. Summary fixtures run the summarizer end to end under
the mock provider and assert that no item cites a record the backend did not supply, that a
request with no source record produces a not-found item, and that malformed output raises
instead of degrading.

Booking contention runs at 2, 10, and 50 concurrent attempts for 30 fresh-slot repetitions
per level after warm-up, each requiring one committed appointment, no duplicate row,
idempotent replay, rollback-safe retry, and post-commit outbox processing.

\IfFileExists{generated/safety_results.tex}{\input{generated/safety_results.tex}}{}
\IfFileExists{generated/booking_results.tex}{\input{generated/booking_results.tex}}{}

The provider manifest records provider, model, interface version, region, temperature,
context limit, timeout, retries, fallback policy, execution date, retention assumption, and
paid-service requirement. Installation commands, checksums, raw output, and
table-generation instructions ship with the archive.

\textbf{Prescription image OCR: a negative result.} An experimental pipeline recognises
photographed prescriptions and matches them against the medicine reference, combining
region detection, a local or cloud recognition backend, a dosage grammar, Bengali numeral
normalization, and fuzzy catalog matching~\cite{du2020,prescriptionocr}. On handwritten
Bangladeshi prescriptions the output is not usable even as a draft. Recognition on cursive
prescriber handwriting is the binding constraint, and fuzzy matching against 67{,}001 brands
turns a partly recognised token into a confident wrong match about as often as a correct
one. Raising the threshold trades those errors for empty results.
Review gating keeps bad extractions out of the medication record, so the cost is wasted
reviewer time rather than clinical risk, but a draft a reviewer has to rewrite is not a
working feature. We make no accuracy claim and publish no benchmark; labelling,
adjudication, and a held-out evaluation would come first.

\textit{Assistant boundary.} A doctor has an active care relationship and a valid
\texttt{specialty\_navigation} grant for the named mock provider (Fig.~\ref{fig:ui-ai}a).
``Patient name: Test Rahim; phone: 01700000000'' becomes ``Patient name: [redacted-name];
phone: [redacted-phone]'' before the schema-gated request. The response offers Dermatology
as an uncertain candidate, says it is not a diagnosis, and keeps manual browsing. Asking
next for a diagnosis and prescription returns a safe refusal. Inputs, authorization state,
schema, intermediate values, and outputs are archived in
\texttt{tests/benchmarks/datasets/worked\_examples.json}.

\textit{Registry containment.} A patient asks the assistant to open the admin dashboard.
The registry holds no administrative route, so resolution yields no destination and the
engine returns its fallback. Nothing depends on the model declining, and a prompt-injected
attempt to name the route directly ends the same way.

\textit{Consent restriction.} A doctor requests a summary for a patient who shared
conditions and medications but not test results (Fig.~\ref{fig:ui-consent}a). The guard
drops the laboratory category, the payload carries a restriction notice into the prompt,
and the summary reports the omission instead of inferring around it. The read goes to the
patient-visible audit table.

\section{Impact}

Medora is a compact test bed for assistive-AI containment, consent state machines, source
traceability, and transaction/event boundaries. The medicine reference
and its build script are reusable away from the platform, and the deterministic mock
provider makes interface and failure tests reproducible without paid credentials. The
registry pattern transfers to any role-scoped application.

The limitations are substantial. Six of the nine groups in Table~\ref{tab:ai-surface} carry
no accuracy or faithfulness measurement, and the structural controls covering them are not
evidence that their outputs are good. The medicine reference is a consolidation of
third-party datasets, two of them website scrapes: it has not been checked against any
regulatory source, its indication text has had no clinical review, and its coverage reflects
when its sources were collected. Structured redaction misses unknown and indirect
identifiers, emergency rules cannot cover every presentation, summaries and specialty
candidates may omit or distort facts, and prescription OCR does not work. Provider
behavior, cost, and retention can change. The concurrency benchmark shows database behavior
in its tested environment, not universal capacity. No clinical trial, regulatory
assessment, penetration test, or independent clinical validation has been done.

\section{Conclusions}

Medora is research software for bilingual patient-held records, appointment coordination,
and assistive AI bounded by construction rather than by instruction~\cite{medorasw}. Its
two reusable parts are the open Bangladesh medicine reference with its published build and
the containment pattern above. Judge it as an inspectable platform for software research,
not as a clinically validated medical system.

\section*{Ethics and data availability}
\label{sec:ethics}

Code is released under the MIT License; annotations, synthetic fixtures, and aggregate
results under CC BY 4.0. The interface figures come from a non-production demonstration
deployment: the patient record belongs to a consenting author and the clinician entries are
test accounts.

The medicine reference consolidates five sources licensed CC0 1.0 (two), Apache 2.0, MIT,
and CC BY 4.0~\cite{bdmeds}, all of which permit redistribution. The corpus is offered under
CC BY 4.0, the most restrictive term in that set, with a notice crediting every source.
Apache 2.0's statement of changes records that generic names were normalized, only the
generic-to-indication mapping kept, and pricing and URL fields dropped. Two sources are
website scrapes whose uploaders did not author the material, which is why the corpus is
called a consolidation and not a register.

The prescription image corpus is not deposited. It is identifiable medical material, its
consent basis is verbal agreement given for an undergraduate software project, no
institutional review board reviewed the collection, and the evaluation it was assembled for
is not part of this release. Consent for a student project is not informed consent for
permanent worldwide publication. The images retain patient and clinician names,
registration numbers, and clinic details, and handwriting is quasi-biometric, so redacting
direct identifiers would reduce re-identification risk without removing it. Any future
deposit needs documented consent or controlled access.
